messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Affective Expression: Crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mateo Reyes is a 25-year-old Colombian American data scientist who presented for an initial intake following what he described, with some difficulty, as "a year of not being able to hold it together." He is single, lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment, and works remotely for a mid-sized analytics firm. The event that brought him to therapy occurred approximately fourteen months ago, when his four-year-old niece, Valentina, was rushed to the emergency room in septic shock following what her parents had initially mistaken for a stomach bug. Mateo had been babysitting her that afternoon.

He had been the one to call 911. He remembers sitting on the kitchen floor with Valentina limp against his chest, her skin mottled and her breathing shallow, while the dispatcher kept asking him questions he could barely process. The ambulance arrived within minutes, but those minutes felt, in his words, "like time had broken." The paramedics worked quickly, and the smell of the room — the particular closeness of sweat and fear, his own and hers — stayed with him long after the hospital corridors had faded. Valentina survived, after five days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Mateo was told she had come very close to dying. He stood in the waiting room and did not cry. He has not cried since.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo found that the memory of that afternoon did not behave like a normal memory. It did not sit in order. He could not reliably reconstruct whether he had called 911 before or after he tried to wake her, whether the dispatcher had spoken first or whether he had. The sequence felt scrambled, and this confused him deeply, because he had always trusted his mind to be precise. What troubled him more was a feeling he struggled to articulate: that the event was so extreme, so outside anything he had known, that it did not feel as though it had genuinely happened to him. Yet when it surfaced — uninvited, often at his desk — the terror returned in full, not as a thought but as a bodily fact, his heart accelerating, his hands going cold, exactly as they had on that kitchen floor.

Mateo works from home, which has offered him a degree of control over his environment, though that control has come at a cost. He keeps his apartment windows closed because the sound of sirens from the street below — common in his urban neighborhood — produces an immediate and overwhelming physical reaction that leaves him unable to concentrate for the rest of the morning. He has structured his workday around this: he begins his most demanding analyses before the city fully wakes. His colleagues have noticed that he declines in-person meetings at the company's downtown office, and his manager recently flagged his increasing isolation from the team as a performance concern. What his manager does not know is that the office building is two blocks from a hospital, and Mateo has not been able to walk past an ambulance bay, schedule a routine physical, or enter any medical facility since the night he stood in that PICU waiting room.

He has come to believe that the safest course is to keep the memory at arm's length. He works long hours, fills his evenings with data, and when something edges toward the surface, he redirects with a deliberateness that has become automatic. He does not allow himself to be angry — not at the situation, not at himself, not at anyone — because he has come to feel that anger, if it were ever released, would be something he could not contain or come back from. When a colleague's child came up in conversation and he felt something sharp move through him, he excused himself and sat in the bathroom until it passed.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a moment at his desk three weeks ago when a neighbor's child was crying in the apartment above him. He sat frozen for forty minutes, unable to work, unable to move, his body insisting it was still on that kitchen floor. He called the clinic the following morning. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly at the end of the intake, is that the memory will never make sense. What he is hoping for, he added after a long pause, is to feel like himself again.
